{"title":"Bud Across America","body":"The goggles fit. That was the strange part. Somewhere in Idaho, two men crossing the country by car for the first time in history stopped long enough to buy a pit bull and strap a pair of driving goggles over his face. The dog held still for it and never tried to shake them off.

Horatio Nelson Jackson was a Vermont doctor who, in the spring of 1903, bet fifty dollars at the University Club in San Francisco that an automobile could cross the country from the Pacific to New York. No one had done it. The roads, where roads existed at all, were wagon ruts. The car he bought for the trip was a Winton touring car with no windshield, and the mechanic he hired to keep it running was a young man named Sewall Crocker.

They left San Francisco on May 23 and pointed the Winton east. Tires shredded. The drive chain snapped. They forded streams, dug out of mud, and navigated by asking ranchers which direction led to the next town. In Idaho, they picked up Bud.

He was a stocky white pit bull, and he climbed onto the seat between Jackson and Crocker as though the spot had been waiting for him. He faced forward, ears pinned flat in the wind. But the alkali dust of the open desert burned his eyes raw, so Jackson found a pair of goggles and fitted them over the dog's broad head. Bud wore them from that point on, every mile, and whenever the Winton sputtered to life he leapt aboard and waited for someone to strap them into place.

The three of them ground east through Wyoming, across Nebraska, through Iowa. Towns turned out to watch them pass, and Bud drew the biggest crowds. People wanted to see the goggled dog more than the car. Jackson wrote that Bud was the one member of the expedition who never lost his temper and never once suggested turning back.

They reached New York on July 26, sixty-three days out of San Francisco. Wire and improvisation held the Winton together. Jackson had burned through far more than fifty dollars in repairs. But they had crossed the continent on four wheels for the first time, and the dog had ridden every mile of it.

Bud's goggles sit in the Smithsonian National Museum of American History now, the leather cracked, the lenses clouded, small enough to fit a dog's face.","cited_sources":["Smithsonian National Museum of American History (artifact and photograph collection)","Dayton Duncan and Ken Burns, Horatio's Drive: America's First Road Trip (2003)"],"uncertain_claims":["Fifty-dollar bet at the University Club in San Francisco (widely reported but not in provided context)","May 23, 1903 departure and July 26, 1903 arrival dates","Winton touring car with no windshield (specific vehicle details beyond provided context)","Drive chain snapping as a specific breakdown","Bud described as stocky and white (inferred from well-known Smithsonian photographs, not stated in provided context)","Jackson's remark about Bud never losing his temper (widely attributed, exact wording varies by source)","Bud's goggles physically surviving at the Smithsonian (provided context confirms photographs are held there; the goggles' presence is separately well-documented but not in the provided context)"]}

BOOK TITLE: Great American Road Dogs
BOOK TOPIC: real, documented dogs that travelled with people who made history
AUDIENCE: general adult reader
TONE: warm and vivid
STORY TITLE: Bud Across America

The context below was gathered by the book's researcher. Treat every fact in it as verified and correct, and build the story around it.

CONTEXT: In 1903 Horatio Nelson Jackson and mechanic Sewall Crocker made the first automobile crossing of the United States, San Francisco to New York. Partway through, in Idaho, they bought a pit bull named Bud, who rode with them wearing goggles against the alkali dust. Photographs are held by the Smithsonian National Museum of American History.

You may add real, well-established detail you are confident about to bring the scene to life. You must NOT invent names, dates, dollar amounts, locations, or quotes that you are not confident are real. If the context is thin, write a shorter, tighter story rather than padding it with invented specifics.

Write this story as 300-500 words of finished prose.

HOW TO WRITE IT:
Find the single most surprising or human thing in the context and build the story around it. One thing told properly beats a summary of everything that happened.
Open on something concrete: the object, the moment, the number that does not sound real. The first sentence decides whether a reader continues.
Use specific detail over general description. Name the thing, the place, the amount. A dog wearing goggles on a dusty road is a story; 'early car travel was difficult' is a summary of one.
Vary your sentences. Mix short ones against longer ones, and vary how clauses join, so the prose does not settle into the same shape line after line. Read it back and listen for a drumbeat.
Vary your paragraphs too. A longer paragraph against a couple of shorter ones. Break where the story turns, not at a word count.
Let the ending land where the story actually ends. Do not append a moral or a lesson. A close that simply stops on the right detail is stronger than one that explains why the story mattered.
Trust the events to carry the weight. Never tell the reader something is amazing, incredible or little-known; show the detail and let them decide.

HARD REQUIREMENTS:
1. Between 300 and 500 words. This is a hard requirement.
2. Real events only. Never fabricate a fact to make the story better.
3. Open with the specific scene or the hook, not with a throat-clearing preamble. Never begin with 'In the world of', 'Picture this', 'Imagine', 'It was a', or a dictionary-style definition.
4. Plain, vivid, conversational prose. No bullet lists, no headings, no markdown inside the story body.
4a. Every paragraph must contain at least 2 complete sentences. Never leave a single sentence standing alone as its own paragraph: it reads as a pull quote, not prose. The only exception is the final paragraph, which may be one sentence that lands the point.
5. Do not address the reader as 'you', and do not editorialize about the book itself.
6. Match the tone: warm and vivid.
7. Do not restate the story title as your first sentence.
8. No adverbs where a stronger verb exists, and no passive voice. Never use a dash as punctuation; use a comma or a full stop.
9. Never join two complete sentences with only a comma.

Return ONLY a JSON object, no prose outside it, no markdown fence:
{
  "title": "the story title, lightly polished if it reads awkwardly",
  "body": "the full story text, paragraphs separated by \n\n",
  "cited_sources": ["publication or outlet you are drawing on, if any"],
  "uncertain_claims": ["any detail a fact-checker should verify"]
}
